label: Facial papules and pustules
q: Acne, rosacea, or something being applied to the face?
lead: The presence or absence of comedones separates acne from everything else, and the history of topical steroid use explains a large share of the rest. Ask what the patient is putting on their face before you ask anything else.

stop.l: Sudden severe nodular acne with fever, arthralgia and malaise
stop.a: Acne fulminans. Systemic corticosteroid first, and introduce isotretinoin only later and at low dose — starting isotretinoin alone can precipitate it.

stop.l: Rapidly progressive facial swelling with pain and visual change
stop.a: Orbital cellulitis or cavernous sinus thrombosis. The danger triangle drains intracranially. Emergency imaging and intravenous antibiotics.

stop.l: Painful, boggy scalp or facial nodules with lymphadenopathy in a child
stop.a: Kerion from inflammatory tinea. Systemic antifungal — topical will not penetrate, and incision and drainage causes scarring.

stop.l: Photosensitive facial eruption with scarring, atrophy and follicular plugging
stop.a: Discoid lupus erythematosus. Biopsy and treat early — the scarring and dyspigmentation are permanent.

stop.l: Ocular grittiness, photophobia or blurred vision with facial flushing
stop.a: Ocular rosacea. Ophthalmology referral. Corneal involvement threatens sight and is underdiagnosed because patients do not connect the eye and the face.

stop.l: Numerous, large or confluent molluscum on the face of an adult
stop.a: A marker of advanced immunodeficiency. Test for HIV and check the CD4 count now - the skin finding is frequently the presenting sign, and destroying the lesions without treating the immunodeficiency achieves nothing.

dx.look: Fine, rough, follicular keratotic papules with variable perifollicular erythema giving a sandpaper or plucked-chicken texture, on the lateral cheeks, outer upper arms, thighs and buttocks; very common, worse in winter and in atopics.
fr: Rough follicular papules with a sandpaper feel
Lateral cheeks, outer upper arms and thighs
Perifollicular erythema
Worse in winter, with background xerosis or atopy
Longstanding and asymptomatic
dx.cf: A clinical diagnosis by texture and distribution; keratosis pilaris rubra faciei (red cheeks in children) is a facial variant. No investigation is needed.
dx.hp: A dilated follicular infundibulum plugged with keratin, sometimes containing a coiled hair, with mild perifollicular lymphocytes.
dx.assoc: Associated with atopic dermatitis and ichthyosis vulgaris; entirely benign and often improves with age, so reassurance is a large part of management.
dx.mgmt: Emollients with a keratolytic (urea, lactic acid or salicylic acid) and gentle exfoliation; a topical retinoid for stubborn cases. Aim for control, not cure.
dx.pat: Lateral cheeks and outer upper arms

dx.look: Inflammatory follicular papules and pustules with post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation and sometimes keloidal scarring in the beard and neck of people who shave, especially those with tightly curled hair; caused by the shaved hair re-entering the skin.
fr: Beard and anterior neck of people who shave
Tightly curled hair (more common in Black men)
Papules and pustules with visible ingrown hairs
Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation
Improvement when shaving stops
ag: A central-face distribution off the beard area
dx.cf: A clinical diagnosis - look for hairs re-entering the skin; the definitive intervention is a change in hair-removal technique. Swab for bacterial folliculitis if pustules dominate.
dx.hp: An ingrown hair re-entering the dermis with a surrounding foreign-body and suppurative folliculitis; transfollicular penetration is characteristic.
dx.assoc: A mechanical problem of shaving curly hair, disproportionately affecting Black men and a common occupational or grooming-policy issue; scarring and keloids can result.
dx.mgmt: Stop or modify shaving (clippers leaving stubble, single-blade, proper technique); topical retinoids and benzoyl peroxide or antibiotic for inflammation; laser hair reduction is definitive.

dx.look: Open and closed comedones are the defining lesion, with inflammatory papules, pustules, nodules and cysts in the seborrheic areas: face, chest, upper back. Adolescent onset. Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation and scarring.
fr: Comedones present — open (blackheads) or closed (whiteheads)
Chest and upper back involved as well as face
Adolescent or young adult onset
Seborrhea
Scarring or post-inflammatory pigmentation
ag: Confined strictly to perioral or periocular skin with a spared vermilion rim
dx.cf: Clinical. In a woman with acne plus hirsutism, irregular periods or androgenetic alopecia, check total and free testosterone, DHEAS and 17-hydroxyprogesterone.
dx.hp: Follicular hyperkeratinization forming a comedo, with perifollicular neutrophilic inflammation and Cutibacterium acnes.
dx.assoc: Consider hyperandrogenism (PCOS, or the HAIR-AN pattern) when acne comes with hirsutism or irregular menses - check androgens; sudden severe acne with systemic features suggests acne fulminans.
dx.mgmt: By severity (Andrews) - comedonal: a topical retinoid; papulopustular: a topical retinoid with benzoyl peroxide and a topical or oral antibiotic; nodular: oral isotretinoin; hormonal therapy (combined OCP or spironolactone) in women.

dx.look: Centrofacial persistent erythema with telangiectasia, and in the papulopustular subtype, inflammatory papules and pustules without comedones. Flushing triggered by heat, alcohol, spice and sun. Phymatous change and ocular involvement in some.
fr: No comedones
Persistent centrofacial erythema with telangiectasia
Flushing with recognized triggers
Age over 30
Ocular symptoms: grittiness, blepharitis
Burning and stinging rather than itch
dx.cf: Clinical. Examine the eyes and ask specifically about grittiness — ocular rosacea is present in a large minority and is missed unless asked about.
dx.dsc: Polygonal vessels arranged in a network over the central face - a helpful separator from other facial eruptions.
dx.hp: Dilated vessels with a perivascular and perifollicular lymphohistiocytic infiltrate, often with Demodex; granulomas in the granulomatous variant.
dx.assoc: Ocular rosacea is common and under-recognized (grittiness, blepharitis) - ask about eye symptoms; flushing triggers include heat, alcohol and spicy food.
dx.mgmt: Trigger avoidance and gentle skin care; topical metronidazole, azelaic acid or ivermectin, and brimonidine for erythema; oral doxycycline (submicrobial) or isotretinoin for severe or phymatous disease.

dx.look: Grouped small erythematous papules, papulovesicles and papulopustules around the mouth, characteristically sparing a clear rim of skin immediately adjacent to the vermilion border. Periocular and perinasal variants. Almost always preceded by a topical corticosteroid, an inhaled steroid, or heavy occlusive cosmetics.
fr: Clear spared rim next to the vermilion border
History of topical or inhaled corticosteroid use
Grouped micropapules rather than discrete large lesions
Young woman
Worsens transiently when the steroid is stopped
dx.cf: Clinical. The single most important intervention is stopping the steroid, and warning the patient about the rebound flare that follows — without that warning they restart it and the cycle continues.
dx.hp: Perifollicular spongiosis and a lymphohistiocytic infiltrate resembling rosacea; not usually biopsied.
dx.assoc: Strongly linked to topical corticosteroid use on the face - the key history; sparing of the vermilion border is characteristic.
dx.mgmt: Stop all topical corticosteroids (zero therapy); topical metronidazole, erythromycin or pimecrolimus, and oral tetracycline for resistant disease.

dx.look: Erythema with greasy yellow scale in the nasolabial folds, eyebrows, glabella and retroauricular areas, without papules or pustules. Often coexists with rosacea, which confuses the picture.
fr: Greasy scale rather than pustules
Nasolabial folds, brows, glabella
Scalp dandruff
Waxes and wanes with season and stress
ag: Discrete inflammatory papules with no scale
dx.cf: Clinical. Consider HIV testing if severe or refractory.
dx.hp: Spongiosis with parakeratosis at the follicular ostia and a superficial perivascular infiltrate.
dx.assoc: Malassezia-driven; severe disease is an HIV marker and is common in Parkinson disease.
dx.mgmt: Topical ketoconazole with a short low-potency corticosteroid or calcineurin inhibitor.

dx.look: Monomorphic follicular papules and pustules, each centered on a hair follicle, without comedones. Malassezia folliculitis is itchy, monomorphic and concentrated on the upper trunk, shoulders and forehead, and is characteristically worse after antibiotics for presumed acne.
fr: Every lesion centered on a follicle
Monomorphic — all lesions at the same stage
Itchy, on upper trunk and shoulders (Malassezia)
Paradoxical worsening on oral antibiotics
Occlusion, humidity, hot tub exposure
dx.cf: Swab for bacterial culture. For Malassezia, KOH from a pustule shows short hyphae and clustered yeast, and a trial of topical or oral azole is both diagnostic and therapeutic.
dx.dsc: Follicle-centered pustules each pierced by a central hair - a perifollicular pattern.
dx.hp: Neutrophils within and around the follicle; Malassezia yeasts (PAS-positive) in the pityrosporum variant.
dx.assoc: Bacterial (S. aureus) versus Malassezia (monomorphic itchy truncal papulopustules, worse with occlusion or antibiotics) - scrape or culture if uncertain. Gram-negative folliculitis follows prolonged antibiotics.
dx.mgmt: Bacterial - topical or oral antistaphylococcal antibiotics and decolonization if recurrent; Malassezia - a topical or oral antifungal, not antibiotics.

dx.look: Abrupt, monomorphic papulopustular eruption without comedones, appearing at an unusual age or in an unusual distribution, often extending to arms and trunk. With EGFR inhibitors, a papulopustular eruption in the seborrheic areas appearing about a week after starting the drug, with xerosis and paronychia.
fr: Abrupt onset in relation to a drug
Monomorphic, all lesions the same age
No comedones
Extension beyond the usual acne sites
Corticosteroid, lithium, isoniazid, anabolic steroid, EGFR inhibitor
ag: Gradual onset over years with comedones
dx.cf: The medication history is the test. With EGFR inhibitors the eruption correlates with tumor response, so treat it with topical antibiotics and retinoids rather than stopping the drug.
dx.hp: A monomorphous folliculitis with neutrophils and few or no comedones - the absence of comedones separates it from acne vulgaris.
dx.assoc: Abrupt, monomorphic papulopustules after corticosteroids, EGFR inhibitors, lithium, androgens, isoniazid or halogens; EGFR-inhibitor rash tends to correlate with tumor response.
dx.mgmt: Address the drug where possible; topical or oral antibiotics and topical retinoids as for acne. For EGFR-inhibitor rash, doxycycline and emollients usually let the drug continue.
dx.pat: Monomorphic, beyond the usual acne sites

dx.look: Follicular papulopustules with fine follicular scaling (pityriasis folliculorum) giving a rough, sandpapery, frosted appearance to the facial skin. Often in the immunosuppressed or after prolonged topical steroid or calcineurin inhibitor use.
fr: Fine follicular white scaling with a frosted look
Immunosuppression or prolonged topical steroid
Refractory to standard rosacea treatment
Burning and itch
ag: Complete response to standard rosacea therapy
dx.cf: Standardized skin surface biopsy with cyanoacrylate, or direct microscopy of a scraping, showing more than 5 mites per square centimeter. Responds to topical ivermectin or permethrin.
dx.dsc: Demodex tails (whitish gelatinous filaments emerging from follicles) with dilated follicular openings.
dx.hp: Numerous Demodex mites within follicles with a perifollicular lymphohistiocytic or granulomatous infiltrate.
dx.assoc: Consider it when a rosacea-like eruption flares on a topical calcineurin inhibitor or steroid, or in immunosuppression; a pustule scraping shows abundant mites.
dx.mgmt: Topical ivermectin, permethrin or crotamiton; oral ivermectin or metronidazole for dense infestation.

dx.look: One to many soft, yellowish papules 1 to 4 mm across with a central umbilication and fine telangiectasia crossing the surface, on the forehead, nose and cheeks of adults over 40. Very common, and constantly mistaken for small basal cell carcinoma.
fr: Yellow color with a central umbilication
Soft on palpation, not firm
A small globule of sebum expressed by firm lateral compression
Forehead, nose and cheeks of an adult over 40
Several similar lesions, unchanged for years
ag: Firm, pearly and translucent with arborizing vessels
Comedones and inflammatory papules elsewhere on the face
dx.cf: Palpate it and squeeze it. Sebaceous hyperplasia is soft and yields a small globule of sebum from the valley of the umbilication; nodular basal cell carcinoma is firm and yields nothing. Dermoscopy shows yellow-white lobules with crown vessels that stop short of the center. Biopsy anything firm.
dx.dsc: Yellow-white lobules grouped around a central umbilication (the cumulus or cauliflower sign) with crown vessels that branch at the periphery but do not cross the center - unlike the arborizing vessels of basal cell carcinoma, which do.
dx.hp: An enlarged sebaceous gland composed of numerous mature sebaceous lobules grouped around a widened central duct that opens at the surface.
dx.assoc: Benign and age-related; also common in solid organ transplant recipients on cyclosporine. Multiple sebaceous neoplasms with atypia should raise Muir-Torre syndrome and prompt a colorectal and urothelial cancer history.
dx.mgmt: Reassurance. Light electrocautery, cryotherapy, laser or trichloroacetic acid for cosmetic concern once the diagnosis is secure; topical or oral isotretinoin flattens them but they return when it stops.

dx.look: Firm chalk-white to yellow superficial papules 1 to 2 mm across on the eyelids, cheeks and forehead, with no surrounding erythema. They do not become inflamed, do not fluctuate and do not respond to acne treatment. Nicking one with a needle releases a hard little ball of keratin.
fr: Chalk-white and firm, 1 to 2 mm
Eyelids, cheeks and forehead
No erythema and no tenderness
A hard keratin ball shells out when the lesion is nicked
Unchanged for months to years
ag: Pustules and comedones elsewhere on the face
Appearing in crops at sites of blistering
dx.cf: Incision with a needle or the tip of a blade and expression of the contents, which both confirms and treats. Milia appearing in crops, at sites of blistering, or on the dorsal hands are secondary - look for a subepidermal blistering disease or preceding trauma rather than treating them cosmetically.
dx.dsc: A uniform whitish-yellow round structure with no follicular opening, no comedo-like plug and no vessels.
dx.hp: A small keratin-filled epidermoid cyst lined by stratified squamous epithelium with a granular layer, sitting superficially in a pilosebaceous follicle.
dx.assoc: Primary milia are inconsequential and occur at any age including the newborn. Secondary milia follow subepidermal blistering - bullous pemphigoid, porphyria cutanea tarda, epidermolysis bullosa, bullous lichen planus - and skin trauma including abrasion, burns, dermabrasion and radiotherapy.
dx.mgmt: Incision and expression of the contents. A topical retinoid for numerous lesions. Nothing else is needed, and antibiotics do nothing.

dx.look: Sharply defined flat-topped papules 1 to 5 mm across and only 1 to 2 mm thick, skin-colored or light brown, round, oval or polygonal, on the face, beard area, dorsal hands and shins. Linear rows mark where the virus was inoculated by scratching or shaving.
fr: Flat-topped rather than dome-shaped
Skin-colored to light brown with no erythema
Linear rows along a scratch or a razor line
Face, beard area and dorsal hands
Many lesions of very similar size and appearance
ag: Central umbilication with an expressible white core
dx.cf: Clinical, supported by dermoscopy showing regularly distributed dotted vessels on a light-brown background. Very numerous, confluent or pityriasis-versicolor-like lesions in an adult should prompt an immunodeficiency assessment including HIV testing.
dx.dsc: Regularly arranged dotted (pinpoint) vessels on a light-brown to yellowish background with a flat, non-papillomatous surface - distinct from the frond-like vessels and thrombosed capillary dots of common warts.
dx.hp: Acanthosis with vacuolated koilocytes and clumped keratohyalin granules in the upper epidermis; papillomatosis and hyperkeratosis are minimal compared with common warts.
dx.assoc: Human papillomavirus, spread by skin-to-skin contact and by autoinoculation. Extensive, refractory facial lesions occur in HIV disease, iatrogenic immunosuppression and epidermodysplasia verruciformis, where squamous cell carcinoma can arise within the lesions on sun-exposed skin.
dx.mgmt: Most resolve spontaneously in immunocompetent people. Stop shaving over them - continued shaving spreads them along the razor line. Topical tretinoin, 5-fluorouracil, imiquimod or salicylic acid; light cryotherapy works but risks dyspigmentation on the face in darker skin.
dx.pat: Face, beard area and dorsal hands

dx.look: Firm pearly dome-shaped papules 2 to 5 mm across with a central umbilication, expressing a white curd-like core when squeezed. Grouped on the face, neck and flexures of children, or in the beard area of adults where shaving spreads them. In advanced HIV disease they become numerous, large and confluent.
fr: Central umbilication with an expressible white core
Firm, pearly and dome-shaped
Grouped, often along a scratch or shave line
Child, or an adult with a new sexual partner or immunosuppression
Surrounding eczematous halo (molluscum dermatitis)
ag: Soft yellow papules with crown vessels in an older adult
dx.cf: Clinical, confirmed by expressing the core or by dermoscopy showing a central white-yellow amorphous lobular structure ringed by radial vessels. In an adult with numerous, large or facial lesions, test for HIV and check the CD4 count - the severity of molluscum tracks the degree of immunodeficiency.
dx.dsc: A central white to yellow polylobular amorphous structure surrounded by a crown of fine radial or punctate vessels that do not cross the center.
dx.hp: A cup-shaped lobular epidermal proliferation containing large intracytoplasmic eosinophilic inclusions (Henderson-Paterson molluscum bodies) that displace the nucleus and discharge into the central crater.
dx.assoc: Molluscum contagiosum virus, transmitted by skin-to-skin contact including sexual contact. Prevalence reaches high levels in advanced HIV disease, where facial and beard-area lesions become large and confluent and cyst-like lesions appear on the ears. Facial molluscum in an adult is a marker of advanced immunodeficiency.
dx.mgmt: In healthy children it resolves spontaneously, so watchful waiting with treatment of any surrounding eczema is reasonable. Curettage, cryotherapy, cantharidin or topical potassium hydroxide when treatment is wanted. In HIV disease the definitive treatment is effective antiretroviral therapy, not repeated destruction.

dx.look: Acne fulminans: an abrupt severe cystic eruption in a teenage boy, with suppuration, hemorrhagic crusting and ulceration of the nodules, plus fever, malaise, generalized arthralgia, leukocytosis and a raised ESR. Acne conglobata: coalescing nodules, cysts and abscesses forming linear mounds over interconnecting sinus tracts, with the trunk more involved than the face, and no systemic upset.
fr: Abrupt severe nodular eruption with ulceration and hemorrhagic crusting
Fever, malaise and generalized arthralgia with the eruption
Teenage boy
Leukocytosis with a raised ESR
Coalescing nodules, cysts and draining sinus tracts on the trunk
Started or escalated shortly after beginning isotretinoin
ag: A handful of papulopustules with no nodules
No systemic symptoms and no ulceration
dx.cf: Clinical, supported by a CBC showing leukocytosis and a raised ESR or CRP. Image painful joints and bones if the systemic picture is marked. Consider the SAPHO and PAPA syndromes when there is sterile osteitis, arthritis or pyoderma gangrenosum alongside the acne.
dx.hp: Dense suppurative and granulomatous folliculitis with follicular rupture, abscess formation and sinus tracts; in acne fulminans there is prominent necrosis and ulceration.
dx.assoc: Acne fulminans is a systemic inflammatory illness with fever, arthralgia, leukocytosis, a raised ESR and sometimes sterile lytic bone lesions. Acne conglobata is occasionally seen with the XYY genotype and with polycystic ovary syndrome, and belongs to the follicular occlusion tetrad with hidradenitis suppurativa, dissecting cellulitis and pilonidal sinus. Both sit on the SAPHO and PAPA spectrum.
dx.mgmt: Systemic corticosteroid first - prednisone, continued for several weeks - and only then introduce isotretinoin at a low dose under steroid cover. Starting isotretinoin alone at full dose in severe nodular acne precipitates the condition. Intralesional triamcinolone for individual nodules; infliximab and anakinra are used in refractory disease. Refer, because this scars permanently.

dx.look: Sharply marginated indurated erythematous plaques with adherent scale and follicular plugging, so a lifted scale shows keratotic spikes on its underside. The centers become atrophic and scarred with permanent dyspigmentation - hypopigmented centrally, hyperpigmented at the rim. Face, ear conchae, external canals and scalp, with scarring alopecia where it reaches hair-bearing skin.
fr: Follicular plugging under adherent scale
Central atrophy and scarring with permanent dyspigmentation
Involvement of the ear conchae and external auditory canal
Photodistributed and worse after sun exposure
Scarring alopecia in the scalp
No comedones and no pustules
ag: Lesions that clear without leaving a trace
dx.cf: Punch biopsy of an active edge with a second sample for direct immunofluorescence, then ANA, anti-dsDNA, a CBC and urinalysis. Treat while you wait - the atrophy, scarring and pigment loss are permanent, and outcome depends almost entirely on how early treatment starts.
dx.hp: Interface (vacuolar) dermatitis with basal keratinocyte damage, follicular plugging, a superficial and deep perivascular and periadnexal lymphocytic infiltrate, basement membrane thickening and dermal mucin; direct immunofluorescence shows a granular IgG and C3 band at the dermoepidermal junction.
dx.assoc: Most cases are skin-limited, but a minority progress to systemic lupus - check ANA, blood counts and urinalysis, and repeat if systemic symptoms appear. Squamous cell carcinoma can arise in long-standing lesions, so biopsy any non-healing area within an old plaque. Smoking worsens the disease and blunts the response to antimalarials.
dx.mgmt: Rigorous photoprotection and smoking cessation, a potent topical or intralesional corticosteroid or a topical calcineurin inhibitor on facial skin, and hydroxychloroquine first-line for anything beyond a single lesion. Methotrexate, mycophenolate or thalidomide for refractory disease.

ctx.s: Perioral dermatitis is predominantly a disease of young women, Fitzpatrick 8e §1

ctx.l: Using a topical corticosteroid on the face
Using an inhaled or nasal corticosteroid
New systemic drug in the last 3 months
On an EGFR inhibitor or other targeted agent
ctx.s: Papulopustular eruption in seborrheic areas within a week, Fitzpatrick 8e §23 Table 23-7

ctx.l: Recent oral antibiotic for presumed acne, which made it worse
ctx.s: Malassezia folliculitis characteristically worsens on antibacterial therapy, Fitzpatrick 8e §26

ctx.l: Known HIV infection, or a CD4 count under 200
ctx.s: Facial molluscum in an adult is a marker of advanced immunodeficiency, Fitzpatrick 8e §27

ctx.l: About to start, or has just started, oral isotretinoin for nodular acne
ctx.s: Isotretinoin started alone at full dose can precipitate acne fulminans, Fitzpatrick 8e §1

find.l: Comedones present — open or closed
find.s: The comedo is the defining lesion of acne and is absent in rosacea, Fitzpatrick 8e §1

find.l: Persistent centrofacial erythema with telangiectasia
Flushing triggered by heat, alcohol, spice or sun
Ocular grittiness, blepharitis or photophobia
Clear spared rim of skin next to the vermilion border
Grouped micropapules around mouth, nose or eyes
Chest and upper back also involved
Monomorphic — every lesion at the same stage
find.s: Polymorphism across lesion stages is characteristic of acne vulgaris, Fitzpatrick 8e §1,§23

find.l: Every lesion strictly centered on a hair follicle
Itchy rather than tender
Greasy yellow scale in nasolabial folds and brows
Fine follicular white scaling with a frosted, sandpapery feel
Nodules, cysts or established scarring
Hirsutism, irregular periods or androgenetic hair loss
find.s: Hyperandrogenism should be sought in adult female acne, Fitzpatrick 8e §1

find.l: Rough follicular papules on lateral cheeks and outer arms (sandpaper feel)
Papulopustules with visible ingrown hairs in the shaved beard or neck
Yellow soft papules with a central umbilication on the forehead or nose
A globule of sebum expressed by firm lateral compression
Firm chalk-white 1 to 2 mm papules that release a hard keratin ball when nicked
Flat-topped skin-colored papules, some in a linear row along a scratch or razor line
Pearly dome-shaped papules with a central umbilication and an expressible white core
Numerous, large or confluent lesions on the face of an adult
find.s: Extensive facial molluscum and refractory flat warts mark advanced immunodeficiency, Fitzpatrick 8e §27

find.l: Lesions are non-inflammatory - no redness, no tenderness, no pus
No comedones anywhere on the face
find.s: The comedo is the defining lesion of acne, Fitzpatrick 8e §1

find.l: Sudden crops of ulcerating nodules with fever, malaise and joint pain
Neutrophil leukocytosis with a raised ESR or CRP
Follicular plugging with adherent scale, central atrophy and permanent dyspigmentation
Involvement of the ear conchae, external canal or scalp with scarring alopecia
Lesions clear when shaving stops and return within days of resuming it
find.s: Andrews' Diseases of the Skin - pseudofolliculitis barbae is mechanical and resolves when shaving stops

find.l: Scaling and erythema also in the glabella, retroauricular folds and presternal skin, worse in winter
find.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §2 - seborrheic dermatitis follows the sebaceous distribution beyond the face

test.l: Stop the topical steroid and observe (with a rebound warning)
test.w: Any perioral or periocular papular eruption in a patient using a topical, inhaled or nasal corticosteroid.
test.p: Clearance over 4–8 weeks after withdrawal, usually preceded by a flare in the first 1–2 weeks, confirms it.
test.n: Failure to improve after 8 weeks off steroid should prompt reconsideration — demodicosis and granulomatous rosacea look similar.
test.x: Warn the patient explicitly about the rebound flare before they stop. Without that warning they restart the steroid during the flare, and the condition becomes chronic. This conversation is the treatment.

test.l: KOH or Gram stain from a pustule, with bacterial culture
test.w: Monomorphic follicular pustules, itchy truncal papulopustules, and any acneiform eruption that has worsened on oral antibiotics.
test.p: Short hyphae with clustered yeast confirms Malassezia folliculitis — treat with an azole, not an antibacterial. Bacterial growth with sensitivities directs antibiotic choice.
test.n: A negative Gram stain does not exclude gram-negative folliculitis in a patient on long-term tetracyclines. Culture specifically for that.
test.x: An acne-like eruption that gets worse on doxycycline is either Malassezia folliculitis or gram-negative folliculitis. Continuing the antibiotic is the wrong move in both.

test.w: Adult female acne with hirsutism, menstrual irregularity, androgenetic alopecia, or abrupt severe onset.
test.p: Raised androgens point to polycystic ovary syndrome, late-onset congenital adrenal hyperplasia, or rarely a tumor. Refer to endocrinology and treat the cause.
test.n: Normal androgens do not exclude a hormonally responsive acne — many women with normal levels still respond to combined oral contraceptives or spironolactone.
test.x: Sample in the follicular phase and off any combined oral contraceptive for at least 6 weeks, or the results are uninterpretable.

test.l: Standardized skin surface biopsy for Demodex density
test.w: Papulopustular facial eruption with follicular scaling that has failed standard rosacea therapy, particularly in immunosuppressed patients.
test.p: More than 5 mites per square centimeter supports demodicosis. Treat with topical ivermectin or permethrin.
test.n: Low counts argue against it, though sampling is operator-dependent.
test.x: Demodex is a normal commensal. Density and clinical context matter, not mere presence.

test.w: When the facial eruption is scarring, atrophic, follicular-plugged or photodistributed — in other words, when discoid lupus or another scarring dermatosis is in the differential.
test.p: Interface dermatitis with follicular plugging and a positive lupus band confirms discoid lupus. Treat early — the alopecia and dyspigmentation are permanent.
test.n: Non-specific histology in a photodistributed eruption should prompt review of phototoxic drugs and polymorphic light eruption.
test.x: Do not biopsy an ordinary acne or rosacea face. Reserve this for eruptions that scar, that are photodistributed, or that fail to behave as expected.

test.l: Firm lateral compression to express sebum, with dermoscopy for crown vessels
test.w: Small yellowish umbilicated facial papules in an adult over 40, particularly on the forehead and nose.
test.p: A soft papule that yields a bead of sebum from the valley of the umbilication, with crown vessels that stop short of the center, is sebaceous hyperplasia. Reassure, or destroy with light electrocautery if it bothers.
test.n: A firm pearly papule that yields nothing and shows vessels arborizing across the surface is a basal cell carcinoma. Biopsy it.
test.x: Sebaceous hyperplasia and nodular basal cell carcinoma sit side by side on the same forehead. The separator is consistency - sebaceous hyperplasia is soft, basal cell carcinoma is firm - and it takes one finger to establish.

test.l: Incision with a needle or blade and expression of the contents
test.w: Firm white non-inflamed 1 to 2 mm facial papules that have not responded to acne treatment.
test.p: A hard white ball of keratin shells out - diagnosis and treatment in one move.
test.n: If nothing shells out and the lesion is inflamed or tender, reconsider - a closed comedo, an early inflammatory papule and a small cyst all behave differently.
test.x: Milia in crops on the dorsal hands, or at sites of previous blisters, are secondary. Look for porphyria cutanea tarda, epidermolysis bullosa or pemphigoid instead of treating them cosmetically.

test.l: Dermoscopy for regular dotted vessels on a light-brown background
test.w: Multiple flat-topped skin-colored facial papules, particularly in a child, a young adult or someone who shaves the area.
test.p: Regularly distributed dotted vessels on a flat light-brown background support flat warts. Stop shaving over them and treat with a topical agent, or wait.
test.n: A negative or nonspecific dermoscopic pattern does not exclude them; the flat morphology and the linear inoculation rows carry more weight than the vessels.
test.x: Shaving through flat warts inoculates them along the razor line, which is why the beard area fills up. Telling the patient to stop shaving over the lesions matters more than which topical agent is chosen.

test.l: Express the core for a molluscum body, and offer HIV testing to any adult
test.w: Umbilicated pearly facial papules at any age, and mandatory in an adult with numerous, large or beard-area lesions.
test.p: A white curd-like core confirms molluscum. In an adult, a positive HIV test with a low CD4 count reframes the whole problem - the definitive treatment is antiretroviral therapy, not repeated curettage.
test.n: A negative HIV test in an adult with extensive molluscum still leaves other causes of immunosuppression to consider - transplant medication, systemic corticosteroid, biologic therapy, hematologic disease.
test.x: Numerous or giant facial mollusca in an adult are treated as a cosmetic nuisance for months while the underlying immunodeficiency goes unrecognized. The skin lesion is often the presenting sign of advanced HIV disease.

test.l: CBC with ESR or CRP, and a systemic assessment before starting any retinoid
test.w: Sudden severe nodular ulcerating acne, particularly with fever, malaise or joint pain, and before starting isotretinoin in anyone with severe nodular disease.
test.p: Leukocytosis with a raised ESR supports acne fulminans. Start a systemic corticosteroid first, continue it for several weeks, and only then add isotretinoin at low dose under steroid cover.
test.n: Normal inflammatory markers do not exclude it if the skin picture is typical - the ulcerating nodular phenotype drives management on its own.
test.x: Starting isotretinoin at full dose in severe nodular acne can precipitate acne fulminans. Steroid first, retinoid later and low. This is the single sequencing error that turns treatable acne into permanent scarring.

test.l: ANA, anti-dsDNA, CBC and urinalysis once a discoid lesion is confirmed
test.w: Every biopsy-proven discoid lesion, and any scarring facial eruption with follicular plugging and atrophy.
test.p: A positive ANA with proteinuria, cytopenia, arthritis or serositis moves this from skin-limited disease to systemic lupus. Refer to rheumatology and treat systemically.
test.n: A negative ANA is common in skin-limited discoid lupus and does not change the skin treatment, which is photoprotection, topical or intralesional corticosteroid and hydroxychloroquine.
test.x: This is not a one-off screen - a minority of localized discoid lupus declares itself systemically later, so repeat it if systemic features appear. And do not wait for serology before treating the skin: the atrophy, scarring and pigment loss are permanent, and every week of delay is written into the face.

flag: Ask what the patient applies to their face, including anything prescribed for a previous problem. Topical corticosteroid on facial skin generates perioral dermatitis, steroid rosacea and demodicosis, and each of these is routinely treated with more steroid.
